title: How to turn a YouTube lecture into practice questions
summary: Use the lecture transcript or your timestamped notes as the source for practice questions.
body_markdown:
Use the lecture transcript or your timestamped notes as the source for practice questions. If an app supports video files, check whether it also accepts a YouTube link before building your study routine around it.


## How can I turn a YouTube video into a quiz I can check?


Pause just before the lecturer finishes a worked example. Write a prediction and the reason for it. Resume and note the timestamp where the reasoning becomes clear. Turn that moment into a question with a short answer key. Where the speaker says “this line,” describe the line from the screen because a transcript alone will leave the reference unresolved.


### Build a quiz from one graph on screen


Imagine a lecture on reading distance graphs. At 04:10 the speaker draws a cyclist’s distance from home against time. At 04:40 she points to a horizontal stretch and says, “What happened here?” The captions contain every word of the question. They leave out the very thing you need to answer it. Before copying any dialogue, give the graph a title in your notes and record what each axis measures, including its units.


For this example, your note might read, “Horizontal axis in minutes, vertical axis in miles from home. Cyclist travels along one straight road. Starts at home, reaches mile six at minute thirty, stays at mile six until minute forty, then rides straight home by minute sixty. Each segment is straight.” Now you have enough information to reconstruct the picture on scrap paper. Keep the timestamp beside the note for checking the answer later.


Start with a question that makes sense with the video closed. “What happened here?” becomes “Between minutes thirty and forty, what happened to the cyclist’s distance from home? How can you tell?” A weak answer says, “The graph went flat.” A stronger answer says, “Ten minutes passed and the cyclist remained six miles from home. The horizontal segment shows the same distance at both ends and throughout the interval.” That answer interprets both axes.


For the second question, ask which moving leg was faster. Both legs cover six miles. Going out takes thirty minutes and coming back takes twenty, so the return is faster. A student who answers “outward, because the line goes up” has confused direction with speed. Put that explanation beside the wrong choice in your answer key. When you miss this item later, you will know exactly which two features of the graph to revisit.


A third question can use a small edit to the drawing. Leave the departure and stop alone, but move the final point from minute sixty to minute seventy. Ask what changes about the two riding speeds. The return now takes thirty minutes, the same as the outward leg. A copied phrase about the steep return will earn no credit here. Label this as your variation so you can distinguish your new endpoint from the lecturer’s original one.


### Decide what belongs in the answer key


Try an ambiguous draft on purpose. “How far did the cyclist go by minute sixty?” could invite either the total length of the trip or a reading from the vertical axis. Split it into two prompts. Ask first for the distance from home at minute sixty, then for the total miles ridden during the hour. The answers are zero and twelve. Write down why both numbers make sense before turning them into choices on a multiple choice quiz.


Keep the graph description on the question side if the goal is interpretation. Hiding the units or the endpoints turns the exercise into a memory test about a particular slide. To practice drawing a graph, reverse the arrangement. Supply the trip in words, draw the segments yourself, then reveal the image or replay the clip. Score the turning points, axis labels and flat interval separately so that a mislabeled axis does not erase evidence of correct reasoning.


### Ask for questions you can check against the recording


Give the tool the short excerpt and your description of the slide together. A prompt for this graph would be, “Use only these trip notes. Ask me one question about direction and one about speed. Give the units in each question. Wait for my answers before showing the working. If a number is missing, tell me which one you need.” Read each question once with the notes covered. Could another student solve it from the information supplied?


Check any proposed key against the timestamp yourself. If the captions say sixteen miles while the plotted point is labeled six, replay the passage and inspect the axis. Leave the calculation out of the quiz until you can settle the discrepancy. For a lecture with several diagrams, keep each figure with its own time range. Combining a caption from one example with the axes from the next can produce a perfectly tidy question about a trip the lecturer never described.


### StudyFetch


StudyFetch can create quizzes from uploaded recordings and videos. A supported file upload does not establish that pasting a YouTube link will work. If the clip cannot be supplied as a permitted file, prepare timestamped notes that retain the relevant visual detail.[Read the product details](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.studyfetch.mobile.v2&gl=US&hl=en) .


### ChatGPT


If you already have a transcript or timestamped notes, ChatGPT study mode can ask questions about the text you provide. Paste the relevant passage and ask for a question that depends on its wording. Check the answer against the lecture before moving on.[Read the product details](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/11780217-chatgpt-study-mode-faq) .


### AI that makes questions from a YouTube lecture?


StudyFetch lists uploaded videos and recorded lectures. To work from a YouTube lecture when direct link support is unclear, use an available transcript or your own timestamped notes. Keep the visual references with your notes so a question about a figure still has a defensible answer.


If you already have a recording file and want a reusable quiz alongside flashcards, StudyFetch supports that combination. If your starting point is a few lines of transcript and a sketch of the axes, try those in ChatGPT Study mode for a question at a time. You can also use the sketch on paper. Fold the page so the answer key stays hidden, redraw the return leg from the changed endpoint, and unfold it only after you have committed to a speed comparison.
